sections.content: You know that *creo que* takes the indicative and *no creo que* the subjunctive (B1 Unit 13), and *dudo que* (B1 Unit 25). The same contrast works with certainty: *estoy seguro de que* and *sé que* take the indicative, while doubt or rejection takes the subjunctive.

items.spanish: Estoy seguro de que tiene razón.
items.english: I am sure he/she is right.

items.spanish: No estoy seguro de que tenga razón.
items.english: I am not sure he/she is right.

items.spanish: Sé que algunas ideas son útiles, pero no estoy seguro de que todas sean realistas.
items.english: I know some ideas are useful, but I am not sure that all of them are realistic.

sections.content: A shortcut: if you could add “and that is a fact” to the English sentence, use the indicative (*Estoy seguro de que tiene razón*); if the truth is in question, as in *No estoy seguro de que tenga razón*, use the subjunctive.
